prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which many atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated together, bringing optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B014, Katori and Ye, as a single-part prize. The question the chair put to us is which criterion should decide between B014 and B016. For me it is whether the physics criterion of a discovery or invention can be stated in one sentence and credited to named people without a gap. For the lattice clock it can: trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength cancels the differential light shift, so a narrow optical transition can be read out with a very large number of atoms. Katori made that proposal and the first realisations, and Ye's group took the strontium clock to record systematic control and developed the many-body clock work. The result has been reproduced in several laboratories and species, and clock-to-clock comparisons near 1e-18 are what make relativistic geodesy, constraints on varying constants and dark-matter searches practical. Reading the round-1 files has narrowed my thinking rather than widened it. Every file that discusses B014 names the same reservation, the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, and none names a credit gap. Every file that discusses B016 names the uncredited HgTe proposal. I take that asymmetry as scientific information about the two cases and not as a vote count. I note that I dropped B042 from my own preferred position in round 1 for reasons of credit and closeness to my own field, and I do not return to it here.
statement.case_against: The overlap argument is real and I do not want to wave it away. A committee can say that the comb made optical clocks countable, that Wineland's ion work started the clock programme, and that the lattice clock is a very successful refinement. Johansson put it sharply: a prize here may reward metrological performance more than a new physical effect. I think the magic-wavelength idea answers this, but only if the citation is written around the lattice trap and many-atom interrogation and not around optical clocks or frequency metrology in general. The second reservation is timing. The SI second has not been redefined, so part of the payoff is still prospective, and I would not let that decide the matter either way. The third is the split between Katori's concept and Ye's accuracy programme, and the claims of Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Lemke and the ion-clock groups. I cannot verify priority dates from the committee files available to me at this stage and am working from recollection. Finally, B016 is a serious candidate with greater conceptual reach, and Mehlig has weakened my earlier view of the 2016 overlap as an objection. My remaining objection to B016 is the credit gap, which I think remains real.

responses.point: Johansson accepts the originality of the magic-wavelength idea but says a B014 prize would reward metrological performance more than a new physical effect, and he wants the committee to decide between a topology-defined discovery and a precision-metrology invention.
responses.response: I accept the framing and answer it directly: I do not think performance and principle can be separated here. The reason the lattice clock reached 1e-18 is the principle. Before the magic wavelength, trapping many atoms meant perturbing the transition one wanted to measure, and afterwards it did not. That is a change in what is possible, not tuning of a known scheme, and it is why the Prize traditionally rewards invention in measurement. I also accept his point that the 2016 prize is distinct from Z2 insulators, and I have moved on that. My difference with him is therefore only on credit. I would resolve his citation fix of tying the experimental part to Molenkamp's observation, but that still leaves Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang unnamed, and with Zhang deceased that gap cannot be repaired by a later prize.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that B016 changed the conceptual framework of a major field while B014 is a transformative instrument for an already well-defined measurement, and that the 2016 prize covers different physics from Z2 insulators.
responses.response: He is right on 2016, and I withdraw the weight I gave to that overlap in round 1: Chern-type quantisation and topological phase transitions are not the Z2 invariant with time-reversal-protected helical edges. I also take his caution that HgTe quantisation is clean only in short edges and that the citation should say observation. Where I still differ is on the weighting. The criterion I use is the Prize's wording on a discovery or invention, not which field has changed its vocabulary more. A conceptual advance is the more significant of the two only if the prize can honestly credit it to the right people. He agrees that the allocation gap is the main weakness of B016. His point that almost every candidate has an omitted contributor is fair, but there is a difference between omitting a later refinement and omitting the group that proposed the platform on which the observation was made.

responses.point: Kroll keeps concept and performance together in one B014 citation and would not extend credit to the wider accuracy race, and he asks the chair whether his Boulder time in Hall's laboratory requires recusal or only disclosure.
responses.response: I agree on both points of substance. A citation that combines the magic-wavelength invention with the realisation at 1e-18 explains why Katori and Ye are a pair, and extending it to the wider race is exactly how we would break the three-name limit and reopen the ion-clock question. I would add that the wording should name the optical lattice clock and not optical clocks. On his disclosure, I would treat his documented link to Hall's laboratory as a disclosure item for the chair to rule on and not as something I can settle for him. I have my own item to settle, set out below, and I would ask that the two be handled by the same ruling so that neither of us is treated differently.

responses.point: Pearce moved from B021 to B014 on attribution and confirmation grounds, and says the citation must be written around magic-wavelength trapping and the accuracy it allowed, not optical frequency metrology in general.
responses.response: I agree with the citation point and with the reason he gives for moving, which is the credit rationale and not the number of first places. It is the same reason I hold B014. I would add that his own doubts about IceCube attribution show why a two-name credit with a clear division of the story is worth a lot: it is the one thing a committee cannot repair after the announcement. I also share his view that the redefinition of the second is a supporting application and not a criterion, and I would be uncomfortable if we deferred the clock for that reason alone.

responses.point: Eriksson asks whether aberration-corrected electron optics (B042), my opening first choice, is physics in the Nobel Prize in Physics sense or an enabling technique closer to chemistry and engineering, and says this was not answered in my ballot.
responses.response: It is a fair question and I will not answer it as an advocate. I disclosed that I work in electron microscopy and am president of the International Federation of Societies for Microscopy, so I should not argue for or vote on B042, and I have removed it from my alternatives for that reason. I will only say that his question is the one a committee should ask, and the credit omission of the scanning-transmission corrector work stands in any case. I note that the same line, enabling technique versus discovery, is what Johansson asks of B014, and I would apply a consistent standard: the lattice clock is an invention that opened a new measurement regime, which is why I stay with it.

uncertainties: Exact priority and chronology of the first magic-wavelength lattice-clock demonstrations, and whether other groups would be argued to share the credit.
Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes once the citation is narrowed to magic-wavelength trapping.
Whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the SI second, which I regard as a supporting argument and not a criterion.
Whether my weighing of the B016 credit gap is too severe given that most candidates omit someone, and whether the HgTe proposal is essential to the observation or only a route to it.
Whether the Tokyo connection described below counts as an institutional conflict for B014, which I leave to the chair's ruling.
statement.conflict_note: Update to my round-1 disclosure. I hold a University of Tokyo fellowship and have long-running exchanges with Japanese universities. To my knowledge Katori is a professor at the University of Tokyo, and I could not verify this against the committee files available to me at this stage, so I treat it as a probable institutional connection to a credited name on B014. My profile records no collaboration, joint publication or supervisory relationship with Katori or Ye. I disclose it plainly and will follow the chair's ruling on whether it requires recusal or disclosure only, in the same way as for Kroll's Boulder link. For B042 I remain conflicted as a microscopist and president of the International Federation of Societies for Microscopy, I do not advocate it and have not listed it as an alternative. Göran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, and that bears on no ballot in my configuration.
